In the year 1910 a new arrangement was entered into by this Government with the various denominations which have charge of these schools. The schools were divided into three classes. A certain standard as to accommodation, equipment, etc., was decided on at a conference between the Government and the different denominations, and the denominational schools which complied with this standard received the highest per capita grant. Then there were departmental 6chools on which the department had stood the original outlay and which were to be brought up to this standard. Then there were the class 2 churcn schools, somewhat inferior in character and quality, which did not draw as large a per capita allowance as the other two classes. This
has increased the grant for education considerably by materially increasing the per capita grant, and by raising the standard of the schools and giving more room, better equipment, and more sanitary methods. Any schools that are under that system are most creditable indeed. The pupils are attending the schools in increasing numbers. We have put a check on capital expenditure during war time, and are simply keeping the schools in repair, although we have been strongly pressed to make capital expenditures by denominational schools at various points where they are really inwant of better accommodation.

I am in sympathy with
the minister in his decision, not to invest-

in any capital expenditure during war time. The Anglican 'bishop of Athabaska, however, has brought to my attention the fact that the increased cost of the necessaries of life is pressing very heavily upon the resources of the church having charge of the schools in his diocese. I understand that he has applied to the department for some recognition of the more difficult conditions. Has any such application been made, and if so, has any recognition been granted ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Requests of that description have come from that bishop and from several other bishops. They say that the present high cost of living is such that the existing per capita grant is not sufficient to prevent them from going behind. In some instances we have been asked to make up the deficit. We have not done so as yet, and we have not promised just at present to increase the grant.
A delegation of representatives of almost all the schools was to have interviewed the department some time ago about this matter, but they did not turn up according to programme. So far we have not passed favourably on any requests for increased assistance.

I do not know that I would suggest to the minister either the assumption of deficits or any very large increase in the grants, but it is a fact that in the north country especially, where the cost of living is at a maximum and transportation very expensive in proportion to the amount of actual supplies consumed, the present conditions bear very heavily upon the schools, and I would respectfully suggest that temporary assistance in the way of a grant be given to them to meet the increased cost of the actual food consumed. It could be a special grant during this period of stress.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Per capita?

It would, of course, be per capita. I think the department would not be doing substantial injustice to the country at large if it specially recognized the schools in that part of the country where the difficulties of carrying on the work are so great.. If the minister saw fit to consider this suggestion favourably in respect of the schools in the Anglican and Roman Catholic dioceses of Athabasca and Mackenzie, assistance would have to be given as soon as possible because supplies for the winter are now going forward. The other schools which are accessible by rail could be dealt with at any time, hut the schools in the more re-

mote outposts of civilization, where the. work is particularly arduous and expensive, have to make their arrangements very far in advance, and it would really be deplorable if, the department having decided to assist them, the assistance came too late to benefit the schools this year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I will consider my hon. friend's suggestion.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

What is the curriculum at these Indian schools? What standard of education are the pupils supposed to reach?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I understand that the Indian schools are conducted on much the same lines as the public schools
9 p.m. of the province. The teachers have to be qualified under the provincial laws, and it is sometimes rather difficult to get them for isolated places, but we do the very best we can. The same subjects are taught as in the public schools, and the same text books are used. The schools are inspected by the public school inspectors, and the pupils are supposed to come up to the standard required by the provincial educational authorities.

Have the pupils any aptitude for arithmetic, reading and writing? How long do they continue their studies, and what are the results obtained in these schools? I do not for a moment suggest that we should drop them, but I wish to know whether the Indians appreciate the educational advantages placed at their disposal. There are small Indian schools in my part of the country, but they are not up to the high school standard. Is it the same in other provinces? Do any of the pupils take up teaching themselves?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It varies with the different provinces. I believe the Indian schools in Ontario have been very successful, the pupils attending school about as long as the pupils at the public schools, and sometimes competing with the white children in the entrance examinations for the high schools.
I do not think the Indian schools in Nova Scotia have been quite as successful, but on the whole we cannot complain very much about the results. In the Maritime Prov-

inces the attendance has not been so good as'in some of the other provinces.

What about the Indian schools in Quebec? Are their studies confined to one language?
Mr. ROC'HE: In the province of Quebec there are twenty-eight day schools. There are 609 boys on the roll, and 647 girls, total 1,256. The average attendance is 802. There are no boarding or industrial schools in that province. In the French districts the Indians are taught in French, and in the essentially English districts in English.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

in Bonaventure county?

speechtext: Yes.

They have put up a new

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

Industrial education is
coming to Ibe recognized as a necessity.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: They have not sent in requests for these schools.

think that the department should take the lead in this matter, the Indians being the wards .of the Government? If the Indians made a success of the industrial life as a result of proper training of the young in their schools, it would be a great credit to the departmeent.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

Perhaps the Indians are
getting more civilized

But civilization goes

Has the minister any statistics to show whether tuberculosis is increasing or decreasing among the Indian tribes of Canada?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I cannot say it is on the increase but, as the hon. member knows, it has been very prevalent. We have been trying to educate them to better sanitary conditions and have endeavoured, by a system of education, to get them to take better care of themselves. I cannot say that so far the diseases has diminished to any great extent, but it certainly has not increased.

The minister sends a doctor among the tribes, treating the Indians for various diseases, and would it not be well to have some one spend some time among them educating them to improve their living conditions and so check the spread of tuberculosis among them? I think that at the present rate it will ultimately destroy them in most places.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We are doing all we can to educate them along sanitary lines.

What is the method of distribution of relief to destitute Indians in the country north- of Edmonton?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The department sends in supplies to the various posts. In some instances the Hudson's Bay Company supplies goods on request of an Indian agent or a missionary, and in some cases the mounted police are utilized for the purpose of distribution.
There are rival . trading posts and trading companies. Does the department recognize the existence of these rival traders, or does it deal with only one trading firm?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
They divide up the order. Sometimes it goes to the Hudson's Bay Company and sometimes to Revillon Freres.

They do not go to one firm only for supplies, each firm gets its share.
Is it divided up in this way, that at one post the Hudson's Bay Company and at another some other trader?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not always, no.

The facts are that, in the north country the Indians trade just as people in other parts of the country trade, some with one firm and some with another. If there are two rival traders at a certain point, some Indians will trade with one and some with another. It is not usual for the Indians to trade promiscuously. They have their ideas in that regard, and, generally, an Indian family will trade with one firm or with the other, and it is recognized that there is that division of the trade. If one of these trading firms is given a monopoly of the distribution of the Government supplies in that locality, they have a huge advantage over their rivals, and, while I suppose the Government is not bound to take cognizance of that condition of affairs, I take the liberty of pointing it out. Of course, I speak only of those who are unquestionably responsible, but if there is any desire to act fairly as between the rival traders, I think it would be fair to make some arrangement whereby each of those rival traders would be responsible for some part of the distribution; otherwise it would be hardly just. Trade rivalry is just as keen as in the far north country as it is in the east, perhaps a little keener. I do not know how far the Government is cognizant of that condition and recognizes it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We recognize where the
Indian trades, and allow him to purchase from the firm he has been accustomed to deal with.

The Micmacs, in my county, live near the mouth of the harbour, and, although, at one time, they went from their summer homes to various camps in the winter, they have now abandoned their old habits in many ways, and live in one settlement contiguous to the mouth of the hanbour. There is a large tract of land reserved there. I should like the minister to state whether this land is held in the same manner as the western lands which belong to the Indians, or whether it is Dominion Government property, on which the Indians are living, and whether the Government are able to deal with it the same as with other property.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Those reserves are held in the same manner as reserves are held in other parts of the Dominion, namely, in trust, and before we can sell the lands, we have to obtain a surrender.

We have not a regular band and chief-just an isolated group of Indians who happen to be living at this particular point. The Government has purchased land in the vicinity of the coal piers where the Indians reside, and the Indians have completely deserted all their old habits and have been engaged largely as freight handlers. Where the Government purchase lands which the Indians are permitted to use, is the purchase made out of a trust fund belonging to the band, or how does the Government make the purchase? Some reservations in the West have been set aside for the benefit of the Indians, but I do not think that is the case in this particular instance.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Some reserves in Nova Scotia have been purchased by Parliamentary appropriation.
Will the minister take a note of this particular case, and I will take occasion to communicate with my correspondent later on, with regard to the changed conditions.
What is the rule of the minister's department in regard to interference by agents in politics, or is there any rule?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There is no different rule in the Indian Department from any other department. The hon. gentleman is aware of the rule laid down by Parliament that officials of the Government', whether they are Indian agents or others, in the employ or on the pay list, are not to engage actively in politics. No different rule is applied to Indian agents than to other officials. Of course, there may be some/ agents who regard their agency work as a side line, drawing very little salary from the Government, and I presume they consider themselves free citizens, but our agents who devote their whole time to the work of the agency are expected simply to perform their duties as agents.

I am somewhat surprised to hear the minister say that there is a rule that there shall be no interference, and that the rule which applies in other departments, applies to this department, because, in the elections held recently in Alberta, one of the homestead inspec-

tors, Ambrose Grey, was a candidate, and ranch inspector George Cloakley, was candidate in another constituency. It is true that Mr. Grey had resigned a few days before the election. Mr. Cloakey resigned, but I am not sure whether it was before nomination. They held their positions so close to nomination day that they cert-ainly must have been using their positions for the purpose of advantaging themselves in the political contest which took place on the 7th June. It is true they were both defeated by rather large majorities, but certainly it was a very plain instance of officials of the Department of the Interior using their position, while under salary, to advantage themselves, at any rate, they hoped to advantage themselves politically, and, if I am not too far out of order, I may say that another appointee of the Government, Dan Minchen, timber inspector in the Grande Prairie country, is now official candidate of the Conservative party in the constituency of Peace River at the deferred election to be held shortly. Here are three instances in which officers of the Land Department have certainly been taking a very active part in provincial politics. Evidently the rule that my hon. friend says applies to all the departments does not apply to the Indian Department as, apparently, it does to the Department of the Interior.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There has been no rule in the past that would prevent a Government Official from accepting nomination at the hands of a political party, as long as he resigned his Government position. If it was wrong for these gentlemen to have accepted nominations, it is to be noted that they resigned their positions in all cases. To my knowledge, no person occupied a Government position and was at the same time a candidate for election. But, if that is wrong, it is a practice that has been in existence for many years. While the member for Edmonton was Minister of the Interior, two homestead inspectors were candidates in elections in my former constituency, one of whom ran against myself and the other against Mr. Glen Campbell. One of these gentlemen occupied his position right up to the time of nomination, but I did not hear any adverse criticism from any hon. gentlemen opposite. If the gentlemen to whom reference has been made are doing wrong, certainly the same thing was done under the administration of the late Government, and without any protest from hon. gentlemen opposite.

It may be just as well to say that one of the gentlemen to whom I refer, who had been a homestead inspector, resigned to become a candidate in the provincial election, was defeated, and .was promptly reappointed by my hon, friend as soon as the election was over. After having used his position during the intervening period of over four years for the purpose of political canvassing, he again becomes a candidate and is again defeated- and I suppose, will again be reappointed. I submit that such a case is simply a scandal:	If my hon. friend thinks that what
took place in former years will justify what is taking place now. I can only say that 1 do not think the public will accept it as justification. Certainly I do not intend to abate my criticism of an action that is absolutely unjustifiable, simply because of previous acts on the part of anybody else. Two wrongs do not make a right. I do not admit it, as a matter of fact, but admitting for the sake of argument that wrong was committed on a previous occasion, I still say that that does not cure the evil, which is that public money is being used for the purpose of maintaining in the field a band of active political agents and canvassers, who, after having suffered defeat at the polls, may be reappointed to their positions, as they, no doubt, expect to be reappointed.

I should think that there is a distinction between the case mentioned by the minister and the case referred to by the member for Edmonton. In this case evidently the political aspirant in Alberta was acting in conjunction with the minister. The minister was probably aware of the purpose of the man's resignation, but he does not say that he will not continue to play the game by reappointing that man. Unless the minister assures us that he is not going to reappoint him he will have to stand convicted of acting in harmony with this manipulator and of being a confederate -I say it not offensively-with him in what we consider to be very improper procedure. The case in question, therefore, is very different from the case the minister has mentioned.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Can you answer for the case that I quoted.

I would have to be convinced that in the other case the then Minister of the Interior had knowledge as to the reason for the resignation before I would consider the cases analogous. Anyway, if any minister has an understanding with an employee that the employee mav

resign the day before nomination, and that if at the election seven days afterwards he is defeated, the minister will re-appoint him, that minister is not using good judgment and should be criticised. If the minister says that he disapproves of that procedure, then we shall know where he stands in the matter. It is of no use to say that such and such a thing was done previously. If I understand the minister aright, his statement is that he has full knowledge of all the circumstances connected with these cases which the member for Edmonton-to our surprise, but not to the surprise of the minister-has brought to the attention of the committee. The minister is well informed in the matter, explains the circumstances and attempts to justify them, and, so far as we know, proposes to re-appoint these men. I think that the minister should be in a position to tell us that he had not knowledge that the men were resigning for the purpose in question, that he was not co-operating with them, and that he will not under any circumstances re-appoint them to their positions.

The hon. gentleman has recently taken a very virtuous turn. I did not know	anything	aboutthese gentlemen having	accepted nominations until their	resignations	camein, except in one	instance.	When
in that case it was brought to my attention that one of my homestead inspectors had accepted a nomination and had not sent in his resignation. I wired him to send it in. I had no knowledge whatever of these candidates being in the field until their resignations came to the department. As to whether these gentlemen intend to apply for reappointment, I know nothing whatever. They may not have any such intention, but when the application comes in, that will be the time for me to say what I shall do. But it is strange that in a parallel case which occurred under the Administration of hon. gentlemen opposite, where a homestead inspector who remained in the field canvassing up to the date of nomination, resigned his position, suffered defeat and was promptly reappointed to his position, no fault was found by hon. gentlemen on the other side. I am not saying that it was so very wrong. At any rate, the hon. gentleman has not pointed out any gross abuse that has arisen out of the candidature of any of these men who resigned their positions, who have been defeated, and concerning whose future intentions I know nothing whatever.

The minister 6ays that I have suddenly become virtuous; he is quite unwarranted in making that assertion. The minister has given us information which he withheld in the first instance, and for which I now give him credit. He did not tell us that he disapproved of a homestead inspector being a candidate and at the same time retaining his position. The member for Edmonton raised that question, but the minister did not say what he was afterwards good enough to tell me- that as soon as he learned that one of the men had been nominated by a political party and had not resigned, he wired him for his resignation. It was in the absence of that information that I made the remark that I did. I have no apology to make for doing so, but in fairness to the minister I say frankly that that eliminates the first part of my criticism. The minister cannot be said to be co-operating with these men at any stage of the game if he had no knowledge as to the purpose of their resignations. But I do say that the minister should assure us that he will not co-operate in the matter by Teappointing these men. It is a brazen thing that a man should become a political candidate, Temain in the public employ as long as he possibly can, and then be reappointed when he is defeated. I say that this should not happen, I care not what any other minister ever did. Other ministers stand on their own reputations and their own records. To reappoint men under such circumstances as these would certainly 'be against public policy. But the Lands Department is administered so viciously and violently along partisan lines that it is scarcely worth our while going into the many things that we might have occasion to refer to.
In the by-election that occurred in Moose-jaw county when the Hon. J. A. Sheppard was appealing to that riding after he had resigned his seat because his name wa4 connected with some of the disclosures in the Saskatchewan commission, that district was alive with his employees; in fact, in some of the small villages you could not get a 'bed at night, because of the number of men pretending to be collecting for seed grain and relief in those places, but really collecting votes. If you put a question on the Order Paper, you do not get an answer and you become discouraged. I should like to have the diaries of those seed grain and relief collectors who were in that county during that election. I could take the minister to a small place called Spring Valley and other stations on

the 'Canadian Northern railway between Avonlea and Gravelbourg where there were four or five of his collectors frightening the people out of their lives toy stating that if they voted against the Conservative candidate everything would he taken away from them and their liens collected, and promising them everything in their favour if they would vote for the Conservative candidate. If their diaries contain a true account of their doings, the minister will find that my statements are correct. Do those collectors keep diaries of what they do?
Mr. ROCHE':	The hon. gentleman is
speaking of men working in connection with the seed grain accounts?
And relief.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: When did this by-election take place?
Last fall.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Just at the time the collectors were out on the road?
Yes.

And because a collector
showed his'nose in a constituency where there was a by-election, the hon. gentleman jumps on the department for allowing a homestead inspector to go into that county during a by-election to collect seed grain accounts.
What a statesmanlike answer to what I have said.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The system that we had adopted a year ago last winter by means of which we were to collect through the elevator companies was not a success, and therefore last summer we opened an office in Moosejaw and established a chief inspector of land agencies there who engaged a staff, largely utilizing the existing staff of homestead inspectors, in order to keep down expense. These men were alloted certain districts, and before there was any thought of a by-election in Moosejaw, they were instructed to collect seed grain personally from the farmers who had got seed grain relief and had failed to pay within the time promised, and no doubt these men were doing certain collections in Moose-jaw county, because there'was a very large amount put out in Moosejaw during 1915. I am not in a position to say whether those men kept diaries that tney sent into the department as to what they did from day to day; in fact I would not be surprised if they did not keep diaries, although in their ordinary work as homestead inspec-

tors they do keep diaries. I will make inquiries in regard to that.

The minister has surely misunderstood what I said. I told him what I thought about the men who had camped in Moosejaw county in order to intimidate the farmers, and the minister says that the Government has lent so much money there and tries to put me in the position of saying that the money should not be collected. I did not say that at all. The money is lent and is repayable and will be repaid. I did not object to any one representing the Government putting his nose into the Moosejaw district; I objected to these men interfering in the by-election. I was speaking about the introduction of petty politics under the guise of those men doing their work in their capacity of collectors. I am not criticising the system of collection at present; I may have something to say about that at the proper time. It is necessary to collect that money, and the minister is making a defence out of the fact that the money should be collected. My point was that the men who should have been busy collecting that money in the proper way were all centralized at one pivotal point, namely, the Moosejaw county seat, whence they could intimidate the farmers of the district into voting for the Conservative candidate.

speechtext: The Estimates of the Post Office Department have been taken up and, as regards the Inside Service, have been passed, so that I am quite within the rule. I am only proceeding to continue to deal with Estimates already begun.

It was distinctly understood that, when the Estimates were allowed

to be taken up, it was not to be held that they had been taken up under the rule. Before the long adjournment we allowed certain Estimates to go through on the understanding that no minister would claim that his Estimates had been taken up under the rule.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My information from
the deputy minister is not that merely one-fourth of the Estimates which were passed, as I understand it, under the arrangement, have been passed, but that the entirety of the Estimates for the Inside Service of the Department have already been passed. If what the hon. member says is correct, I, of course, do not want to break any understanding that has been arrived at, but my information is that with the exception of this one Estimate, the Post Office Estimates have all been passed:

If the minister will . iook at Hansard of February 1 at page 353, he will find that the statement of my hon. friend from -South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) is verified. The report reads:
Supply-Interim Vote.
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rainville in the chair.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	We will not go into
any particular estimates, hut we will give you what you want; we will give you a quarter of the total amount in these estimates.
Sir George Foster:	They are just the same
as the usual estimates.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier :	Ves.
Sir George Foster:	We have usually put
through the vote for civil government.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	I have no objection to
your putting through the estimates that you want to put through, but you know there is a rule that on Thursday and Friday the Speaker leaves the chair without any motion, and the House can only take up such Supply as is to be taken into consideration. If we were to pass all the estimates to-day, when we begin after the adjournment we could not take up any of the estimates upon any day, and therefore we cannot consent to that. But if it is understood that the rule will not apply, then we will pass the estimates.
Sir George Foster:	I think that can easily
be understood on both sides of the House.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier:	All right; go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If that is all that was done, I do not claim that these Estimates were begun, but my information-and I have sent to make quite sure-is that [DOT] all the Post Office Estimates for the Inside Service have already been passed, and that there remains but the Outside Service. If that be correct, it means that these Estimates have been proceeded with otherwise than under that arrangement. Of course, if any information is shown to be mistaken,
I do not want to insist upon going on with these Estimates.

If no Post Office Estimates have been put through since the two months' adjournment the minister would not be in order in going on with these Estimates, and my recollection is that no Post Office Estimates have been put through since the adjournment. Certain Estimates were put through before the adjournment to enable the Prime Minister to go to England, on the distinct understanding that no advantage would be taken of that technical violation of the rule.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All I can say is that
the officer tells me he understands that the whole of the Inside Service Estimates were put through one evening by the Minister of Finance. I cannot undertake myself to say positively whether that was so or not, and if objection is taken I suppose I shall have to yield to it.

The members of the
House have certain rights in regard to moving resolutions on going into Committee of Supply, and we shall be deprived of one opportunity of moving a resolution on the motion to go into Supply if the minister goes on with these Estimates to-night. The whole object of the new rule was to give members an opportunity to move a resolution on the motion for Supply. My recollection is that the Post Office Estimates have not been before the committee, technically speaking, and consequently they cannot be taken automatically on a Thursday or Friday.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the Votes and Proceedings of the 20th of April it appears that Post Office Estimates were passed as follows: Salaries $842,820, Contingencies $125,000. That seems to confirm what the officer told me. I am not invoking the fact that before the two months' adjournment
10 p.m. one-quarter of the Estimates were passed.
The estimates the minister has quoted were .for civil government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, but not on the occasion to which my hon. friend has referred.

The 20th of April
was on a Friday.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The question is, have
these Estimates been taken up? I understand that if they were taken up we have a right to go on, and they must have been

taken up because on that day the committee consented to go on with them.

On the motion of
Sir Thomas White for Committee of Supply on April 20, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
I do not object to the House going into Committee of Supply. I understand that we are to take up the Civil Government Estimates, but this will not interfere with rule 17 (c) which requires that the Estimates of any department shall be first taken up on a day other than Friday.

That was the very day.
It has been admitted, I think, by both sides of the House that civil government form one Estimate and the regular Estimates another, for the purpose of this rule in Tegard to going into Supply. The taking up of Civil Government Estimates does not mean, technically speaking, that we are going into Supply on the General Estimates. I think the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition have agreed as to that on several occasions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If there is any objection to our proceeding with these Estimates to-night I have no desire to go on with them. I have no desire to violate any understanding.
It is a little more than an understanding. The leader of the Opposition called attention to the rule on that occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, then, I have no desire to 'break any rule. Unless, however, there is some objection other than the formal one I shall be glad to go on.

The objection I have is this: Members of Parliament not on this side alone, but on the other side also, were protected by the new rule in their privilege of presenting a resolution on going into Supply. If we go on with these Estimates we shall be depriving ourselves of one opportunity of making such a resolution, and we have not many opportunities left.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. member does not see his way to withdraw his objection I shall have to acquiesce.

In justice to the Postmaster General, would the minister inform the House as to his exact position at the present time? Those who read the Montreal papers have seen that the Postmaster General offered his resignation to the Prime Minister, but it was not accepted. Then the Hon. Mr. Blondin undertook, with General Les-sard, to raise a regiment in Quebec, and met with substantial success all through

the province. When conscription was adopted by the Cabinet we were told that Hon. Mr. Blondin would discontinue his recruiting efforts. The papers now announce that he is coming back to Ottawa to take over his former department and to be Acting Secretary of State. I think it is in the public interest, and only doing justice to the Postmaster General that the House should know exactly what is his position.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know that 1 should be in order in answering my hon. friend. If I am not entitled to proceed with my Estimates there is nothing before the committee. If it is not in order for me to answer questions, I do not see how it is in order for hon. gentlemen to ask me questions. However, I have no objection to stating that the Hon. Mr. Blondin is still on service, and the fact of my being here as Acting Postmaster General indicates that the newspaper report that he had returned to resume his duties as Postmaster General is incorrect.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Doherty, the House adjourned at 10.15 p.m.
Friday, June 15, 1917.
